fields.why: The tested claim and case summaries are proportions (77% vs 29%, 37% hospitalized); the '14 days shorter' is a single process-time difference between two investigations, not a distribution of a measured health quantity. A's continuous is defensible only by reading that difference (or the descriptive median age) as a claim-bearing outcome.

The only inferential contrast compares cases' 77% with a published FoodNet population survey estimate (29%) treated as fixed, which the brief names as a fixed referent. A's pair is defensible if the untested 2022-vs-2020 investigation-time contrast is taken as primary.

For the FoodNet contrast the values are only set side by side with a p-value; no difference or ratio is computed. 'Absolute' holds only for the secondary '14 days shorter' contrast, and testing a difference is not computing one.

The 2022 vs 2020 contrast compares the duration of two investigations (a process measure), not a health outcome at two time points. A's before/after is defensible under the literal 'two time points compared' rule, which the brief could restrict to outcome data.

PulseNet is described as 'CDC's molecular subtyping network for foodborne disease surveillance', so CDC surveillance system and sentinel/network are both defensible (it is national, not sentinel, so the former fits better). A's 'other' for FDA traceback is marginal: traceback informed the source qualitatively and produced no analyzed quantities.

Cases were identified through national PulseNet surveillance across all states, with the 11 states being where cases occurred rather than a sampling frame; the title says 'United States'. A's subnational is defensible under 'multistate networks'.

brief_issues: The brief does not say how to set setting for a multistate outbreak detected by national surveillance, nor whether process measures (time to source identification) count for outcome_types, before/after design or comparison.
